articles.title: Roraimense aprovada no concurso do Itamaraty toma posse como diplomata | G1
articles.standfirst: Antes de conquistar a aprovação, Nínive Memória enfrentou quatro reprovações, cumpriu promessa ao Flamengo e deve seguir carreira descoberta em mapa astral.
articles.summary: Antes de conquistar a aprovação, Nínive Memória enfrentou quatro reprovações, cumpriu promessa ao Flamengo e deve seguir carreira descoberta em mapa astral.
articles.body:
Nínive Memória toma posse como diplomata — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A roraimense Nínive Thaís Verde Sampaio Memória, de 28 anos, tomou posse como diplomata no Ministério das Relações Exteriores nesta quarta-feira (4). O concurso para a carreira de diplomata do Itamaraty é considerado um dos mais difíceis do Brasil .

💼 Diplomatas são servidores públicos que integram o Ministério das Relações Exteriores (Itamaraty). Entre as funções, está representar o Brasil em reuniões internacionais, negociar acordos com outras nações e prestar assistência aos brasileiros no exterior.

Nínive conquistou uma das 60 vagas oferecidas em um concurso que teve mais de 10 mil inscritos e cinco dias de provas. Segundo o Itamaraty, a nova turma tem a maior participação proporcional feminina da história, com 45% de mulheres.

🌐 Ela exercerá o cargo de terceira-secretária , que marca o início da carreira diplomática. O salário inicial é de R$ 22.558,56.

Para alcançar o resultado, foram quatro reprovações, uma perda pessoal e até uma promessa feita ao Flamengo. A jovem conta que decidiu ser diplomata ainda na infância. Aos 12 anos, fez um mapa astral na internet que apontou que ela tinha uma " personalidade diplomática ". Curiosa, passou a pesquisar sobre a profissão e decidiu que aquela seria carreira que seguiria.

A confirmação da aprovação, publicada no dia 24 de junho, foi acompanhada de uma mistura de surpresa e emoção. Nínive disse que estava cautelosa para não criar expectativas até ver a lista definitiva.

"Vi que minha nota tinha subido, mas não queria criar muitas expectativas, sabe? Quando enviaram a planilha [dos aprovados] pude gritar sozinha no elevador. No apartamento chorei, pulei, explodi um tubo de confete (ganhei para estourar quando passasse) e liguei pros meus familiares, depois comemorei com amigos", relembrou.

Para fazer o concurso não é exigida uma formação específica, mas é necessário ter algum diploma de curso superior reconhecido pelo Ministério da Educação. Mas, no caso de Nínive, ela cursou Relações Internacionais na Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU), em Minas Gerais.

Após concluir Relações Internacionais, em 2021, Nínive se mudou para Brasília e começou a se preparar para a carreira diplomática. Ela tentou o concurso em 2022, 2023, 2024 e 2025. Em maio de 2023, passou a se dedicar exclusivamente aos estudos, com apoio financeiro do pai.

A preparação foi interrompida pela morte da melhor amiga e de uma tia que considerava como irmã mais velha. Depois de meses afastada, retomou os estudos e, em 2025, buscou equilibrar a preparação com a saúde física e mental.

Ela chegou à segunda fase pela primeira vez em 2024, mas não conseguiu a aprovação no ano seguinte, quando teve dificuldades na prova de espanhol.

"Nas primeiras vezes achei justo não passar, eu não tinha um bom nível ainda. Só fiquei muito decepcionada em 2025, pois tinha estudado bem e estava mais confiante. Depois de algumas semanas de descanso, peguei meu sentimento negativo e usei para estudar", contou.

Para a edição de 2026, ela encontrou no futebol uma motivação extra. Nínive prometeu que estudaria pelo menos três horas e meia por dia durante 100 dias caso o Flamengo conquistasse o Campeonato Brasileiro e a Libertadores . O time venceu as duas competições , ela cumpriu a promessa e, no fim, foi aprovada.

Após avançar novamente para a segunda fase em 2026, Nínive intensificou a preparação e passou a estudar oito horas por dia nas duas semanas anteriores às provas. Ela destaca que não existe uma fórmula única para a aprovação, mas considera a persistência fundamental. Durante a trajetória, também buscou acompanhamento psicológico para lidar com as frustrações e a pressão dos estudos.

Nascida e criada em Roraima, Nínive estudou os primeiros anos na Escola Estadual São José, em Boa Vista, e depois passou pela rede privada. Ela lembra com carinho de uma professora que a ensinou a escrever resumos e a ajudou a conquistar um dos três primeiros lugares em uma competição escolar.

Após concluir o ensino médio, foi aprovada em primeiro lugar em Relações Internacionais na UFRR, mas escolheu cursar a graduação na Universidade Federal de Uberlândia (UFU), para morar longe da família e ganhar independência. Aos 17 anos, mudou-se para Minas Gerais e, depois de formada, foi para Brasília.

articles.title: Temporal causa estragos em Rifaina e Guariba | G1
articles.standfirst: Municípios registraram queda de árvores e desabastecimento de energia.
articles.summary: Municípios registraram queda de árvores e desabastecimento de energia.
articles.body:
A chuva forte que atingiu a região de Ribeirão Preto (SP) na tarde deste sábado (7) causou estragos, principalmente, em Rifaina e Guariba . As pancadas duraram 15 minutos, em média.

Há relatos de queda de árvores e desabastecimento de energia nas duas cidades. Vídeos aos quais a EPTV , afiliada da TV Globo, teve acesso, mostram a força dos ventos.

O estado de alerta emitido pela Defesa Civil do Estado de São Paulo apontava a possibilidade de rajadas de até 70km/h.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, não havia informação sobre feridos ou desabrigados.

A Defesa Civil informou que, nas próximas horas, o tempo volta a ficar nublado e são esperadas novas pancadas de chuva no decorrer da noite, de forma isolada e sem se prolongar por muito tempo. Há risco de novos temporais, mesmo que de forma rápida.

Em nota encaminhada à EPTV , a CPFL informou que a CPFL Paulista informa que a chuva provocou impactos pontuais sobre a rede elétrica nos municípios.

"Equipes foram rapidamente mobilizadas e estão atuando para restabelecer a energia aos clientes afetados, em segurança, no menor tempo possível".

Em Rifaina, uma árvore caiu sobre um carro e outra bloqueou uma rua.

Chuva forte causa estragos e queda de árvores em Rifaina, SP — Foto: Redes sociais

Segundo a Prefeitura de Guariba, na Praça Central, algumas árvores foram derrubadas pela força dos ventos. Também houve o deslocamento de telhas da ETEC, que atingiram o portão de uma residência.

"Felizmente, não houve danos à residência nem registro de vítimas. Os trabalhadores que estavam no local realizaram a retirada das telhas", diz em nota.

Ainda segundo a prefeitura, na Avenida Milton Rocca teve destelhamento e rompimento de fios.

"A Prefeitura Municipal, por meio da Defesa Civil Municipal, segue acompanhando as ocorrências e adotando as medidas necessárias para garantir a segurança da população e a recuperação dos locais afetados".

A orientação é que os moradores redobrem a atenção, evitem áreas com árvores ou estruturas danificadas e, principalmente, não se aproximem de fios caídos ou rompidos.

articles.title: Servidor público cai no chão após raio atingir moto a poucos metros | G1
articles.standfirst: Jesus de Nazaré da Silva, de 65 anos, contou que caiu devido ao susto e não foi atingido pela descarga. Caso foi registrado em Guaraí, na região centro-norte do estado.
articles.summary: Jesus de Nazaré da Silva, de 65 anos, contou que caiu devido ao susto e não foi atingido pela descarga. Caso foi registrado em Guaraí, na região centro-norte do estado.
articles.body:
Um raio atingiu uma moto em Guaraí, na região centro-norte do Tocantins, neste sábado (7). O servidor púbilco Jesus de Nazaré da Silva, de 65 anos, estava parado ao lado do veículo e acabou caindo no chão. O momento foi registrado por uma câmera de segurança.

📱 Clique aqui para seguir o canal do g1 TO no WhatsApp

Em entrevista ao g1 , Jesus contou que o episódio aconteceu por volta das 12h20, quando parou no local e conversava com um conhecido. Segundo ele, o raio atingiu o retrovisor de sua moto. Ele não foi atingido diretamente pela descarga elétrica.

“Não senti nada, só vi aquele clarão. Quando deu aquele clarão, acho que foi do susto, aí eu caí de costas”, relatou.

Câmera de segurança registrou raio atingindo retrovisor e derrubando servidor público — Foto: Reprodução/Guaraí Notícias

O servidor, que trabalha na Agência de Transportes, Obras e Infraestrutura do Tocantins (Ageto), contou que bateu a cabeça no chão de terra e sofreu apenas um arranhão no braço.

“Levantei rápido, também não senti nadinha, nem dor de cabeça, nem nada, só ralou o braço um pouquinho”, contou.

Apesar do susto, a motocicleta continuou funcionando e teve apenas o retrovisor direito danificado. Jesus conseguiu sair do local conduzindo o veículo e voltou para sua casa.

O caso chamou a atenção nas redes sociais por causa do nome do servidor. Internautas fizeram comentários bem-humorados sobre a coincidência. "Que bom que Jesus está bem", brincou uma usuária.

Ao falar sobre o episódio, Jesus agradeceu por ter escapado sem ferimentos graves. "Mas isso aí é um livramento de Deus, né? Bom demais, graças a Deus que me livrou dessa aí e vai me livrar pra sempre, com fé em Deus", afirmou.

A moto teve o retrovisor danificado mas continuou funcionando — Foto: Arquivo pessoal/Jesus de Nazaré

articles.title: Duelo de MCs Piauí: 16 finalistas disputam vaga no nacional | G1
articles.standfirst: A programação gratuita começa às 17h30 com duelos de improviso entre classificados de várias regiões.
articles.summary: A final do Duelo de MCs Piauí reúne 16 artistas na Praça Pedro II, em Teresina, para definir o representante do estado na etapa nacional do torneio em Belo Horizonte.
articles.body:
Parnaíba, Picos, Valença, Oeiras, Capitão de Campos e Teresina estarão representadas na final estadual do Duelo de MCs, que reúne 16 artistas neste sábado (7), na Praça Pedro II, em Teresina.

A competição vai definir quem representará o Piauí na etapa nacional do campeonato, realizada em Belo Horizonte.

A programação começa às 17h30 e contará com duelos de improviso entre os classificados nas batalhas realizadas em diferentes regiões do Piauí.

Entre os finalistas está o MC Mecin, que participa da disputa pela quarta vez. Em entrevista à TV Clube , ele afirmou que o desempenho nas batalhas vai muito além da criatividade do momento e exige dedicação diária.

"Tem que ler muito, estudar, como se fosse uma escola também. Tem que treinar. Às vezes, todo dia. Toda hora que eu vou tomar banho, boto uma batidazinha e vou rimando", contou.

Segundo o organizador Marcelo da Silva, a final demonstra a força da cultura hip-hop no Piauí.

"São 16 MCs selecionados, MCs de Parnaíba, Picos, Valença, Capitão de Campos, Oeiras. Está essa junção do Piauí inteiro para poder fazer acontecer da melhor forma e muito bonito", afirmou durante entrevista à TV Clube.

A programação é gratuita e aberta ao público. Ao longo da tarde e da noite, os participantes vão se enfrentar em duelos de improviso até a definição do campeão estadual.

articles.title: Delegado relata medo e superação após diagnóstico de filha com Down | G1
articles.standfirst: Delegado declarou que se sente inspirado pela filha. Ele espera que a menina vença adversidades e afirmou que tem aprendido com ela.
articles.summary: Delegado declarou que se sente inspirado pela filha. Ele espera que a menina vença adversidades e afirmou que tem aprendido com ela.
articles.body:
Marco Antônio Maia emocionou a internet ao publicar uma homenagem sobre sua filha Maria Rita, de 2 anos — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

O delegado de Goianésia , na região central de Goiás, Marco Antônio Maia, relembrou a preocupação quando recebeu o diagnóstico de síndrome de Down da filha em uma postagem que comemorava os 2 anos de vida da menina. Marco admitiu que ficou triste e preocupado com o futuro. "O primeiro preconceito que precisamos superar é o nosso. Não era falta de amor. Era medo do desconhecido", escreveu.

Ainda de acordo com o delegado, a filha Maria Rita foi diagnosticada com trissomia do cromossomo 21 (T21) ainda na gestação. Ele declarou que, com o passar do tempo, percebeu que havia sofrido mais pelo que imaginou do que com a realidade que viveria com a pequena.

O delegado explicou que acompanhou as terapias e superações da menina e disse que chegou a se sentir inspirado pela força da filha.

"Minha pequena guerreira! Sua rotina de terapias, estímulos e desafios me ensina todos os dias sobre determinação, paciência e amor. Cada conquista, por menor que pareça aos olhos dos outros, é uma imensa vitória para nós", descreveu Marco.

Ao g1 , Marco Antônio contou que, além de Maria Rita, tem outras três filhas: Valentina, Gabriella e Marcella, de 12, 8 e 5 anos, respectivamente. Ele e a esposa, Aline Lobo, estão casados há 16 anos.

Marco Antônio e Aline tem quatro filhas. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal/Marco Antônio

Ainda na publicação, Marco falou que espera que a filha seja feliz, respeitada e amada. Marco explicou que tinha a missão de ajudar a menina a vencer todas as adversidades, mas admitiu que é ele quem tem aprendido com ela.

"Eu achava que minha missão seria ensinar você a enfrentar o mundo. Mas foi você quem me ensinou a enxergá-lo de outra maneira. Papai te ama infinitamente", concluiu.

articles.title: Data protection law faces scrutiny: The key concerns explained
articles.summary: India's new data protection framework was introduced with a clear objective: to give citizens greater control over their personal information and make
articles.body: India's new data protection framework was introduced with a clear objective: to give citizens greater control over their personal information and make organisations accountable for how they collect, store and use it. But as the government moves towards implementing the law, a growing debate has emerged over whether safeguards designed to protect individual privacy could also affect investigative journalism, access to public records and government accountability.The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, is facing a legal challenge from the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), which represents 21 news organisations. The association has approached the Supreme Court, arguing that several provisions of the law and its accompanying rules could restrict journalistic activities, compromise confidential sources and undermine the Right to Information (RTI) framework.The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre on October 27 and listed the matter for further hearing on November 17. The government, meanwhile, has indicated that it is open to amending the rules or even the law itself if necessary to address concerns over press freedom.The challenge has brought an important question into focus: Where should the line be drawn between an individual's right to privacy and the public's right to know? While one view holds that constitutional protections and judicial scrutiny can address competing interests, another argues that journalism needs explicit statutory safeguards.What is the DPDP Act and why was it introduced?Parliament passed the Digital Personal Data Protection Act in August 2023, establishing a legal framework to regulate the processing of digital personal information.The legislation came against the backdrop of India's rapidly expanding digital economy, where personal information has become central to everyday activities. Banking transactions, online shopping, digital payments, social media accounts, healthcare services and government welfare schemes all involve the collection and processing of personal data.While this has made services more accessible, it has also increased the risks of data breaches, identity theft, unauthorised sharing and misuse of personal information.The need for a comprehensive data protection framework gained importance after the Supreme Court, in its landmark 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, recognised privacy as a fundamental right under the Constitution.The DPDP Act seeks to establish obligations for organisations handling personal data and provide individuals with rights over how their information is processed.The ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) notified the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, on November 14, 2025, following consultations with stakeholders.According to a Press Information Bureau (PIB) backgrounder published on November 17, 2025, the government received 6,915 inputs during the consultation process. These included suggestions from startups, micro, small and medium enterprises, industry bodies, civil society organisations, government departments and citizens.The government described the framework as citizen-centric, with an emphasis on consent, transparency, accountability and responsible use of digital personal information.What does the law provide?The Act revolves around two key categories: Data Fiduciaries and Data Principals.A Data Fiduciary is an organisation or individual that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data. This could include a bank collecting customer details, an e-commerce platform storing purchase histories or a company maintaining employee records.A Data Principal is the individual to whom the personal information belongs.The legislation requires Data Fiduciaries to obtain consent before processing personal data, except in specified circumstances where processing is permitted under the law. Such consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous.Individuals must also be informed about the purpose for which their information is being collected and how it will be used.The Act provides Data Principals with several rights, including the right to access information about the processing of their personal data, seek correction and erasure, withdraw consent and raise grievances. They can also nominate another person to exercise their rights in certain circumstances.Organisations are required to implement reasonable security safeguards to protect personal information. In case of a data breach, they must notify the Data Protection Board of India and affected individuals in accordance with the prescribed framework.The legislation also provides additional safeguards for children's data. Organisations are generally required to obtain verifiable parental consent before processing the personal data of children below 18 years. The law also restricts tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children, subject to specified exemptions.The framework provides for the Data Protection Board of India, which is responsible for examining complaints, conducting inquiries and determining penalties for non-compliance.The financial consequences can be significant. Under the Act, failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach can attract a penalty of up to Rs 250 crore. Violations relating to breach notifications and obligations concerning children's data can attract penalties of up to Rs 200 crore.Why are news publishers challenging the law?The most prominent concern raised by the DNPA is the absence of a specific exemption for journalistic activities.The association argues that the law does not adequately distinguish between the commercial processing of personal information and its use for reporting matters of public interest.Journalists frequently rely on personal information while investigating allegations involving public officials, companies, financial transactions and government decisions. Such investigations may require access to records and information without informing the person concerned in advance.For instance, a journalist investigating alleged irregularities in the assets of a public official may need to examine financial records, property details and business associations. Seeking consent from the individual before collecting or using such information could alert the subject to the investigation and potentially compromise the reporting process.Similarly, time-sensitive reporting and live television coverage often involve the use of information about individuals without obtaining prior permission.The DNPA has argued that the notice, consent and data-erasure requirements under the DPDP framework could make such activities difficult.In its petition, the association has challenged Sections 7, 17(2), 18, 19, 27, 29, 36, 37 and 44(3) of the Act, along with Rules 16, 17 and 23 of the DPDP Rules.It has argued that the provisions fail to recognise journalistic activity as a distinct category deserving protection under the Constitution and could affect journalists, ground reporters, whistleblowers, citizen journalists and RTI activists.The association has also raised concerns over the possibility of individuals withdrawing consent and seeking erasure of their personal information. It fears that this could be used to pressure news organisations into removing reports or altering digital archives, even when the information is relevant to public interest.The challenge is not about denying individuals the right to privacy. Rather, it concerns whether the law provides sufficient safeguards for reporting that requires the collection and publication of personal information in the public interest.What do legal experts say about press freedom?The debate has produced differing assessments of whether journalism needs a separate exemption under the legislation.Advocate Adhitya Srinivasan believes the constitutional protection enjoyed by the press and the nature of the legislation could allow competing interests to be resolved through judicial scrutiny."Freedom of press is so well-entrenched in our Constitution, so I really don't think that the DPDP Act is going to materially impair investigative journalism," Srinivasan said.He argued that Parliament had deliberately chosen a framework that articulates core principles without becoming overly prescriptive, leaving courts to undertake a balancing exercise when competing rights come into conflict."This is hardly unusual, and far from being problematic, it is just a deliberate choice that Parliament has made," he said.Srinivasan also pointed out that the legislation was not necessarily intended to restrict reporting. In his assessment, its objective could instead be to discourage practices such as doxxing and voyeurism.On the question of whether journalism requires an explicit exemption, he said: "I don't think journalism needs an explicit exemption under the DPDP Act, but I suppose it wouldn't hurt."Advocate Mayank Arora, however, takes a more cautionary view, arguing that the absence of an express exemption could create significant difficulties for public-interest reporting."I think yes, there is a strong likelihood that The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, could affect investigative journalism because it does not expressly exempt public-interest reporting from its consent requirements," Arora said.He argued that journalists investigating allegations involving public officials may need to examine financial records, ownership details and private communications, and seeking consent from the individuals concerned could defeat the purpose of an investigation.Arora also warned that the law could produce a chilling effect, with journalists avoiding investigations into powerful individuals because of potential complaints, litigation costs and regulatory uncertainty."The real danger here is not necessarily direct censorship, but a chilling effect on journalists," he said.He maintained that an explicit exemption would provide stronger protection for legitimate investigative reporting while preserving safeguards against misuse of personal information.RTI amendment: Why is Section 44(3) under scrutiny?Another major point of contention is Section 44(3) of the DPDP Act, which amends Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information Act, 2005.The earlier provision allowed public authorities to withhold personal information if it had no relationship to public activity or interest, or if its disclosure would cause an unwarranted invasion of privacy. However, it also allowed disclosure where a larger public interest justified making the information available.The amendment changes the wording of the exemption to cover information relating to personal information.Critics argue that the revised provision removes the earlier balancing mechanism between privacy and public interest, potentially making it more difficult for citizens to access information held by public authorities.The implications could extend to information concerning public officials, government decisions and the functioning of public institutions.For example, a journalist or an RTI applicant seeking information about the assets or official dealings of a public servant may encounter questions over whether the information falls within the personal information exemption.The central concern is that information could be withheld even when its disclosure has a legitimate bearing on public accountability.The government, however, has defended the amendment.In a PIB release issued on August 20, 2025, MeitY said the DPDP Act sought to recognise both an individual's right to protect personal information and the need to process such information for lawful purposes.The ministry maintained that the amendment to the RTI Act was intended to balance the right to privacy with the right to information.Srinivasan believes concerns over the amendment may be overstated."This suggestion that the RTI amendment weakens the right to access public information is in my view a red herring," he said.He argued that the amendment does not prevent public authorities from disclosing personal information when the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm."By way of the substitution, personal information cannot be given to citizens as a matter of right. This does not, however, stop a public authority from allowing access to information (even personal information) if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm," he said.Arora, on the other hand, believes the amendment substantially weakens the express public-interest protection previously available under the RTI Act.He pointed to cases involving recruitment records or alleged favouritism in government departments, where information could reveal corruption involving public money but may now be denied under the broader personal-information exemption.He also questioned why the earlier public-interest qualification was removed if authorities could continue to disclose information after weighing competing interests.Could government powers affect journalistic sources?The DNPA has also questioned provisions that give the government powers to seek information and restrict access to certain information.Section 36 empowers the Centre to call for information from Data Fiduciaries or intermediaries for specified purposes. The association has argued that the provision could affect the confidentiality of information held by news organisations.Journalists often depend on confidential sources, including whistleblowers and individuals who share information about alleged corruption, corporate wrongdoing or administrative irregularities.The possibility of sensitive information being sought by the government, the association argues, could discourage people from sharing information with journalists.This could have implications for investigative reporting, particularly when sources fear that their identities or communications may be exposed.Another provision under challenge is Section 37, which empowers the government to direct the blocking of access to information in specified circumstances.The association has questioned the scope of these powers and the safeguards available against their possible misuse.The broader concern is whether provisions intended to protect personal information could also create restrictions on the circulation of news and information.Is the Data Protection Board independent?The composition and functioning of the Data Protection Board of India have also come under scrutiny.The Board is expected to serve as the principal adjudicatory institution under the law. It will examine complaints, conduct inquiries and determine penalties against organisations that fail to comply with the framework.However, questions have been raised about the government's role in the appointment of its members and the extent of its institutional independence.Under the notified rules, the selection process for the chairperson and members involves a search-cum-selection committee comprising senior government officials and government-nominated experts.The DNPA has challenged provisions concerning the Board, including Sections 18 and 19 of the Act and Rule 17 of the Rules.The concern is that an institution responsible for adjudicating disputes involving both private organisations and government departments should have adequate independence from the executive.Government agencies themselves process large amounts of personal information while implementing welfare schemes and providing public services. This makes the independence of the regulatory institution an important aspect of the data protection framework.What has the government said?The Centre has defended the legislation, maintaining that its primary objective is to protect citizens' privacy and regulate organisations that collect and process personal information.Union electronics and information technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw has rejected suggestions that the law is intended to restrict journalistic freedom.On October 29, Vaishnaw said that freedom of the press was constitutionally guaranteed and that the government had no intention of affecting it.He also indicated that editors and media professionals could engage with the government to discuss their concerns.The government's position is that the obligations under the legislation are primarily directed at Data Fiduciaries, such as banks, telecom companies and insurance providers, rather than journalists as a category.In a report published on October 31, The Times of India quoted senior MeitY officials as saying that the Centre was open to changing the rules and, if necessary, the law itself to ensure that the framework did not become an impediment for journalists and media organisations.Officials maintained that journalists and media houses do not fall within the category of Data Fiduciaries merely because they undertake reporting activities.They also indicated that exemptions could be incorporated into the rules to address concerns over journalistic work.Arora, however, believes government assurances alone cannot provide adequate protection."Assurances must be backed by statutory provisions and enforceable laws and rules," he said.He argued that an express exemption would offer a stronger legal foundation for independent journalists and digital publishers, rather than leaving the matter dependent on administrative assurances.When will the law come into effect fully?Although the DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025, the government has provided a phased implementation timeline to allow organisations to prepare for compliance.According to the enforcement timeline published by MeitY, certain institutional provisions, including those relating to the establishment of the Data Protection Board, came into force in November 2025.The amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act also came into effect as part of the initial phase.Other provisions, including the main obligations governing the processing of personal data, are scheduled to come into force 18 months after the November 13, 2025 notification. This places the key implementation date at May 13, 2027.The transition period is intended to give organisations time to establish consent mechanisms, strengthen security systems and put procedures in place to comply with the law.For news publishers, however, the legal uncertainty is likely to remain until the Supreme Court examines the challenge and the government clarifies whether additional exemptions will be introduced.What happens next?The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre on October 27 after hearing the DNPA's challenge. A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana agreed to examine the petition and listed the matter for November 17.The court did not grant an interim stay on the challenged provisions without hearing the government's response.The Centre will now have to respond to the questions raised by the association, including the absence of a specific journalistic exemption, the amendment to the RTI Act and the powers granted to the government under the legislation.The government has also indicated that it is willing to consider changes if required.The outcome could have implications beyond news organisations. It may help determine how privacy rights, access to public information and the freedom to investigate are balanced under India's digital regulatory framework.The larger question: Can privacy and public interest coexist?The debate over the DPDP Act reflects a difficult balance between two important principles.On one hand, individuals should have control over their personal information. Financial details, health records, identity documents and private communications should not be freely collected, shared or used without appropriate safeguards.On the other, access to information and the ability to investigate matters of public interest are essential to accountability. Journalism and the RTI framework often require the examination of information that may be personal in nature but has wider public significance.The challenge, therefore, is not simply about choosing between privacy and press freedom. It is about creating safeguards that protect both without allowing one to become an obstacle to the other.The Supreme Court's examination of the law will be important in determining how these competing interests are reconciled.For citizens, the implications go beyond newsrooms and technology companies. They concern how much control individuals have over their personal information, how easily they can access information about public institutions and how effectively those in positions of authority can be held accountable.As India moves towards a more data-driven economy, the task before policymakers is to ensure that stronger privacy protections do not come at the cost of transparency and the public's right to know.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Wisconsin trooper released from ICE custody after 'dramatic experience'
articles.summary: A Wisconsin state trooper who came to the U.S. from South Africa as a teen was released from ICE custody. He has a work permit and an asylum case.
articles.body:
A 21-year-old South African-born Wisconsin State Patrol trooper who was detained Nov. 5 by federal immigration agents was released from custody Nov. 6, according to his attorney.

Attorney Marc Christopher confirmed to the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel that Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe, who was traveling to visit family with a valid work permit, had been released from the Dodge County Jail and was awaiting a ride from his supervisor, the head trooper in Tomah.

Christopher said Van Der Merwe was released under an order of supervision, which requires him to periodically check in with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He will also likely be subject to electronic monitoring, potentially through an application on his cellphone rather than an ankle bracelet.

Christopher said he plans to speak with Van Der Merwe to discuss the next steps in his case. He expects Van Der Merwe will eventually share his experience publicly but wants to give him time to readjust following his release.

"I just told him I wanted him to get back, get reacclimated, just get settled, because I know he's gone through a very dramatic experience," Christopher said.

Van Der Merwe came to the U.S. from South Africa with his family on visas at age 14, Christopher said. His family has been waiting seven years for their asylum case to be heard.

Earlier, Christopher slammed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for detaining a Wisconsin law enforcement officer who has permission to work, saying he was "flabbergasted" by the agents' decision to use its resources to target Van Der Merwe.

"I almost can't even believe that they would be so brazen as to do this. But they are," Christopher said. "There's no reason for them to detain him other than to indiscriminately pick up as many people as they can."

Van Der Merwe, who lived in New Mexico with his family, wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but could not because he was not a permanent resident, Christopher said. He graduated with a degree in criminal justice in New Mexico, then researched states where he could do similar work with his status and found Wisconsin.

Van Der Merwe was living in Onalaska and working in Tomah for the Wisconsin State Patrol over the past year. His work authorization is valid until 2030.

Attorney disputes ICE's assertion about legal status

ICE's argument is that Van Der Merwe – as a teenager in the U.S. with his family – overstayed his visitor's visa.

"He entered the country in March 2019 with legal permission to stay until September 2019. In defiance of our nation's laws, he overstayed his admission," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement. "Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the U.S."

Christopher pushed back on that assertion.

"That is just absurd and ridiculous," Christopher said. "They've been here lawfully. They have been waiting for their application to be adjudicated and to be decided by immigration."

The family, who are White South Africans, had applied for asylum on the grounds they were persecuted. A family member had been attacked, Christopher said.

Van Der Merwe did not decide to come to the U.S. himself, as he was brought by his parents, and he chose a career in law enforcement to serve his new country, Christopher said.

ICE agents detained him Nov. 5 at the Dane County Regional Airport just after he went through security, Christopher said. He was traveling to visit his family in New Mexico. Agents handcuffed him, shackled his legs and put him in a van and drove him to Dodge County Jail, which holds ICE detainees.

Christopher said it seems that the Transportation Security Administration tipped off ICE when he bought his ticket, and agents met Van Der Merwe at the airport. Christopher has heard of ICE making arrests at the Milwaukee and Appleton airports through similar tip-offs, he said.

Lawyer hopes Congress changes the way ICE can operate

Under the Trump administration, ICE has not been setting bond for detainees voluntarily unless a judge orders it. Trump administration policy changes have made many detainees ineligible to even seek bond and leave detention.

Christopher said he hopes Wisconsin's congressional delegation takes note of the case and institutes changes to the way ICE can operate. He was critical that ICE would use its resources to arrest Van Der Merwe, then hold him in custody.

"You're going to use your resources to go after this guy? You're going to use our tax dollars to detain this guy? It doesn't make any sense," Christopher said.

As part of its summer surge in street arrests in Milwaukee, ICE arrested a 20-year-old Milwaukee man, Giovanni Sosa, who had lived in the U.S. since age 4 . In detaining him, ICE gave him paperwork that said – at age 4 – he had overstayed his visa. Sosa spent a month in detention at the Dodge County Jail as he waited for the chance to post bond.

Sophie Carson is a general assignment reporter who reports on religion and faith, immigrants and refugees and more. Contact her at scarson@gannett.com or 920-323-5758.

articles.title: A £1.8 million estate was left in dispute after a London property developer married two women in Las Vegas five years apart without divorcing his first wife; the legal battle began after his death
articles.summary: An accountant and property developer died, leaving an estate valued at around £1.8 million, but two women claimed to be his wife after he married them in
articles.body: An accountant and property developer died, leaving an estate valued at around £1.8 million, but two women claimed to be his wife after he married them in Las Vegas five years apart. James Dinsdale married dentist Victoria Fowell in 2012 and beautician Margaret Dinsdale in 2017. He had not divorced his first wife before the second ceremony, making the later marriage void.Dinsdale died from cancer in October 2020, aged 55, without leaving a will. His estate was due to pass to Fowell and his son under intestacy rules. According to the Independent, Margaret asked the High Court to recognise her as a spouse for an inheritance claim and award her a share of the estate.James Dinsdale married two women in Las Vegas without divorcingDinsdale married Dr Victoria Fowell, a cosmetic dentist based in St Albans, at the Little White Wedding Chapel in Las Vegas in June 2012. The couple did not divorce. Five years later, he married Margaret at the Chapel of the Flowers on the same street, about 600 metres from the first venue.Margaret’s barrister told the court that she and Dinsdale had met in 2008 and become friends before starting a romantic relationship in 2014. They moved in together the following year. He told the court she did not know he remained married to Fowell and only discovered the earlier marriage after his death. Her barrister said she believed Dinsdale was divorced when they married.Margaret sought a share of James Dinsdale's £1.8 million estateDinsdale died in October 2020, aged 55, after cancer. He had built a property development business based around central London and left no will. Under intestacy rules, his estate was due to be shared by Fowell and his adult son, William Dinsdale. Margaret brought a claim under the Inheritance Act 1975, seeking reasonable financial provision from the estate. Her claim was for at least half of the £1.8 million fortune. She argued that she should be treated as a spouse because she had married Dinsdale in good faith, believing he was no longer married to Fowell. Her claim was against Fowell and Dinsdale's son William.High Court recognised Margaret as a spouse for her inheritance claimAt a preliminary High Court hearing, Margaret's barrister Jonathan Davey KC said she had been Dinsdale’s primary carer during his final illness and had looked after him around the clock. The court heard that they had been together for six years and planned to have children. He said, "She and James had a relatively lavish lifestyle, which was funded by his wealth and she was entirely financially dependent on the deceased.”“Dr Fowell and William Dinsdale were not being financially maintained by the deceased at the time of his death."Master James Brightwell was told it was not disputed that Margaret should be considered a spouse under the 1975 Act. He made a declaration to that effect for the purposes of her claim.Further hearing to decide how James Dinsdale's estate is dividedThe declaration did not decide how much Margaret would receive. Master Brightwell directed that a further hearing should consider how the estate would be divided between Margaret, Fowell and William. The court also heard differing accounts of money Margaret had already received. It was alleged that she had received £375,000 from the estate or sums derived from Dinsdale.Her barrister disputed that figure, saying she had received only £20,000 from his pension. The judge allocated Margaret £50,000 from the estate to help meet her bills and legal costs while the case continued. Her projected legal costs were estimated at about £175,000 overall.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court proceedings and media reports. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the marriages, financial arrangements, or inheritance claims. articles.title: Brooklyn tenants rented an apartment from someone falsely claiming to own it, then faced a $120,000 judgment sought by the former landlord; after the building was sold again, a New York court dismissed that claim
articles.summary: Renting an apartment from someone who falsely claims to own a property can lead to unexpected legal problems, even for tenants who believe they have a
articles.body: Renting an apartment from someone who falsely claims to own a property can lead to unexpected legal problems, even for tenants who believe they have a valid lease. In Brooklyn, Deborah and Demetris Jones found themselves facing a $120,000 claim after renting an apartment from a woman who had fraudulently represented herself as its owner. The dispute continued even after the building changed hands, but a New York court has now dismissed the claim, finding that the former property owner no longer had the right to pursue it after selling the building and transferring its legal rights.In a decision issued on November 5, 2026, and dated November 6, 2026, the New York Supreme Court in Westchester County ruled in favour of the tenants in 131 Vernon Elite, LLC v. Jones. The judgment, available on Justia, examined whether a former landlord could enforce an earlier agreement against tenants after selling the property and assigning its rights in a separate landlord-tenant proceeding to the new owner. The court concluded that the former owner could no longer enforce the agreement under these circumstances.How the tenants became involved in the ownership disputeDeborah and Demetris Jones moved into Apartment 3 at 131 Vernon Avenue in Brooklyn on February 15, 2018. They had signed a lease with Sepideh Homayoonfar, who falsely presented herself as the property's owner.The ownership dispute was later addressed in a separate court proceeding. A February 28, 2023, decision declared a fraudulent deed that purported to transfer ownership to Homayoonfar's deceased husband invalid. This restored ownership to Shaul Amzalag, who subsequently transferred the property to 131 Vernon Elite LLC on March 29, 2023.Vernon Elite began legal proceedings against residents of the building, including the Joneses, by commencing a holdover proceeding on April 22, 2023. On September 1, 2023, it filed a separate lawsuit seeking $163,000 for use and occupancy from September 1, 2017. The claim included periods before the Joneses had moved in and before Vernon Elite became the property's record owner.The agreement that led to a $120,000 claimOn October 30, 2023, Vernon Elite reached a settlement agreement with the tenants. Under the arrangement, the Joneses agreed to vacate their apartment and return the keys by February 18, 2024.The agreement also stated that if the tenants complied with the terms of a separate landlord-tenant settlement, the company would waive outstanding arrears and discontinue its claim against them. However, if they breached the agreement, Vernon Elite could seek a judgment. Before the agreed move-out date, another major change occurred. On February 6, 2024, Vernon Elite sold the building to Abraham Gelbstein and transferred its rights in the landlord-tenant proceeding to him.The Joneses did not leave by February 18. However, on March 29, they reached a new court-approved agreement with Gelbstein, who had replaced Vernon Elite in the landlord-tenant case. Under the new arrangement, the tenants could remain until May 31, 2024, in exchange for two payments of $2,000 for their continued occupancy. The Joneses made both payments and vacated the apartment by the agreed date. Despite the sale and transfer of its legal rights, Vernon Elite continued pursuing its earlier claim. It sought a judgment of $120,000, along with interest and legal costs, based on the previous settlement. A judgment was signed on September 23, 2024.Why the New York court dismissed the claimIn August 2026, the Joneses, through new legal counsel, asked the court to vacate the judgment. After hearing oral arguments on August 31, the court set it aside and held an inquest on September 17, hearing testimony from a member of Vernon Elite and Demetris Jones. The central question was whether Vernon Elite still had the legal right to enforce the original agreement after selling the property and transferring its rights to Gelbstein.The court explained that ownership of property includes several rights, such as the right to possess it, control it and receive it back when someone occupying it leaves. When Vernon Elite sold the building, it transferred its ownership rights to Gelbstein. This meant that Vernon Elite no longer had the right to demand the apartment keys or take possession of the property when the Joneses were supposed to leave. The court also noted that the company had separately transferred its rights in the landlord-tenant proceeding to the new owner.Gelbstein subsequently negotiated a fresh agreement with the tenants, allowing them to remain for additional time in exchange for occupancy payments. The court found that this new agreement replaced the earlier landlord-tenant arrangement between Vernon Elite and the Joneses. It also rejected the idea that the former owner could continue demanding money based on an agreement connected to possession of a property it no longer owned or controlled.What the ruling meansThe court noted that Vernon Elite could potentially have protected its financial interests through an arrangement with the buyer when selling the building. However, no such protection was established in the case.It also observed that Vernon Elite had benefited from the original agreement because it was able to sell the property before the tenants' departure date without an escrow being held or credits being given to the buyer because of their continued occupancy. The judgment and order, dated November 6, 2026, dismissed the case, with the court concluding that Vernon Elite no longer had the right to enforce the agreement against the Joneses.The decision highlights how selling a property and transferring associated legal rights can affect an ongoing landlord-tenant dispute. It also shows why the terms of a property sale and the handling of existing tenant agreements can become important when ownership changes during legal proceedings.You use AI every day. articles.title: Houthis say at least 25 killed in Saudi air strike
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, has not commented.
articles.body:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.

There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.

Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.

The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.

The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.

Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.

The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.

The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.

A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.

The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.

Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.

The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.

The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.

Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.

A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

articles.title: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn’t expect a smooth ride
articles.summary: Laura Kuenssberg talks to government insiders about the prime minister opening the conversation about the UK rejoining the EU.
articles.body:
Déjà vu? The Eurostar has been booked. Strategic leaks of draft agreements have started.

The EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier is warning the UK it can't have it all and it will not be able to rejoin its single market "à la carte".

Naturally, there is even a row about smoky bacon crisps – an argument between the UK and EU about food labelling has become a classic of the genre. Remember the bendy banana? Or the so-called sausage war between Boris Johnson and Emmanuel Macron?

It's a clash between those arguing it's worth swallowing some new rules to ease trade with the continent, or those whose message to Brussels is, "hands off our snacks" - even though we are not actually in the EU anymore.

Andy Burnham's big moment with the bloc top brass is fast approaching - the second annual EU-UK Summit since the UK's withdrawal from the EU takes place in Brussels on 20 November.

That meeting is not supposed to be about whether the UK might one day go back in. The prime minister has suggested that is his long-term ambition - but is he really ready for what is to come?

First, Burnham inherited the broad deal that's likely to be signed. The UK and EU were originally meant to mint a new and, they hope, improved agreement back in May, then in July, and well, political upheavals mean one thing for getting things done – delay.

But that means the outlines of a new agreement have been clear for many months, an approach based on "closer alignment" as Sir Keir Starmer proclaimed to us at the start of the year.

So if the prime minister hails agreement, spare a thought for those who started the work to get it this far many months ago.

One source familiar with the negotiations told me, "They are 90% there", with agreements designed to make life easier for food producers, a deal on emissions trading which could help manufacturers, and new arrangements for youth visas (although it's understood there is still haggling over putting a cap on the numbers).

An EU source close to the process said: "The bone of contention is a cap – we proposed 150,000, the UK proposed 50,000 – but we would expect to reach a compromise", even though it has been "very tense" on both sides.

A last-minute call from the EU to cut tuition fees for its students is expected to be parked for now with more months of discussion to come. Another fine tradition - agree what you can, but file some tough stuff away for future chat.

There are dilemmas too on the EU's so-called "Made in Europe" plans – draft laws to protect its industries from being hammered by Chinese competition. The purpose is clear – to help the economy grow, with the prime minister quoting figures that suggest closer ties to the EU without going back in could add 0.4 percent to GDP.

But as the tabloid-friendly row over salty snacks illustrates, making it easier to do business with the bloc doesn't come without a cost, and a political awkwardness.

Talking to my colleague, the BBC's Business editor Simon Jack this week, the prime minister admitted the UK would have to follow more EU rules. "That's where we've ended up," Burnham acknowledged.

And whatever your feelings on the matter, that lands us slap-bang back in the middle of the eternal dilemma of the relationship between the UK and the European Union.

How much control is the UK willing to lose in the hope of bigger wins? Even when it comes to a relatively limited number of important issues that are on the table in the current discussions?

The prime minister has scrapped the limits of this troubled conversation, not just suggesting a closer relationship with the relatively dry and technical changes being discussed right now, but dangling the possibility of going back into the bloc one day.

Suggesting freedom of movement again, unlimited immigration for Brits who want to live or work on the continent and vice versa. That's after repeated promises, including from him, that that sometimes toxic debate would not be reopened.

What is he up to? It seems the prime minister's main line of thinking is that with problems like long passport queues and red tape for business it is right and proper to try to sort them out.

That is after all, what Rishi Sunak and then Sir Keir Starmer tried to do.

But his willingness to contemplate going a lot further is based on a belief that the public's attitude has shifted – if you look at polling it does suggest that a majority of voters support going back into the EU .

It just so happens his own long-time conviction is to go back into the bloc one day. And that idea chimes not just with many Labour activists and members, but also with the Lib Dems, Greens and SNP – whose voters he'd be only too happy to peel off.

But hang on, don't let Burnham's easy-breezy style mask that just casually mentioning he is open to us going back into the EU in the run up to this summit is a huge and difficult thing. Whatever relationship he truly wants to seek, and even those involved in the conversations aren't quite sure he is even sure, don't expect a smooth ride from the EU.

In an interview you can see tomorrow, the EU's chief negotiator last time, Michel Barnier, told me the UK cannot pick and choose the relationship "à la carte".

If we wanted to go back in, he told me, the UK could forget the famous rebate, and there is no way to be in the huge trading bloc, the single market, without accepting freedom of movement.

One government figure told me, even now dealing with the EU there are "lots of very warm words, but quite a lot of arms folded".

An EU insider told me the mood has certainly changed. "There is big scope getting closer to the EU, but nobody wants it to be toxic… we wonder, does he know what he is doing?"

Last time round, the majority of businesses, with some notable noisy outliers, were keen to stay in the EU. But after several years having to make the relationship work, and spend money on rearranging how they do business, that might not translate into such solid support if the prime minister does choose to pursue a return to the EU.

One prominent business figure explains: "You're a langoustine exporter from Ullapool? Yes, please. You are manufacturing and making that car? Yes, get me back in. You're a drugs manufacturer? Well, sort of, yes and no. You're in financial services? We've spent the money. Do we want to unpick this?"

There are prominent backers of the idea of a return to the EU, if Burnham himself decides to make that case. The former Chancellor Rachel Reeves and the London Mayor Sadiq Khan make the case as well.

We've already talked about the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP, and Plaid Cymru being up for it, as are many Labour MPs and ministers.

But the political risks of arguing for a return to the union are, frankly, enormous. Labour is divided, just as the country could be, whatever the current polls suggest.

One former Labour minister told me, "the prime minister wants us to go back in, but it is a very hazardous route", saying of the party's broadly pro-European rank and file: "Nobody wants to criticise Andy, but if it blows open they won't all be in the same place".

One cabinet minister's eyes rolled so violently when I asked if they fancied another referendum they nearly went into the back of their head. And it is a safe bet that if the prime minister really decides to pursue a return that there'd be a ferocious pushback from the other side.

The Conservatives and Reform are already howling with protest about the deal expected to be signed this month.

Kemi Badenoch criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum" adding, "he is not going to get a better deal… it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand."

Meanwhile Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door", and said Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".

And you can expect similar financial arguments to be made as last time round. Vote Leave was always only too happy to have noisy clashes over the cash the UK paid to be part of the EU – that £350m – the gross contribution, not the net.

But every argument about the amount reminded the public that the UK did spend millions, even if the figure was officially judged as misleading.

While EU leaders might want to be helpful to Burnham, the Czech prime minister's comments on the issue were rather unhelpful. Asked recently if he'd like to see the UK go back his answer was, "Yes, of course – we need more money".

There could be enormous opportunity for the economy, important support for the UK's security, and a boost for the prime minister's backing among some voters if he does indeed end up deciding he will make the case for the UK to rejoin the European Union.

But it would be a heck of a gamble. A decade ago, a relatively popular prime minister named David Cameron with expert communication skills wanted to reset the UK's relationship with the EU. That blew up his leadership, unleashing a series of political disasters that saw him off, and dogged his party for years.

Andy Burnham is a relatively popular prime minister too, also confident in his ability to communicate with you, and serious about improving our ties with the EU. But in his party, there are those preaching caution about opening this conversation.

The successes or failures of the impending summit will give him, and the rest of us, a taste of what might lie ahead.

articles.title: Airstrikes kill 27, mostly women and children, near Yemen's capital, Houthis say
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Airstrikes hit homes in a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, on Saturday, killing at least 27 people and injuring 36 others, most of them
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Airstrikes hit homes in a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, on Saturday, killing at least 27 people and injuring 36 others, most of them women and children, according to a spokesperson for the Houthi-run Health Ministry.Speaking to The Associated Press (AP), ministry spokesperson Anees al-Asbahi said the death toll could rise as rescue teams continued searching through the rubble. He accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the strikes on al-Shariya village.Houthi military spokesperson Brigadier General Yahya Saree later claimed that the group had launched attacks against Saudi Arabia in response to the strikes on the village and a separate deadly attack on a market in southwestern Yemen on Friday.However, the Houthi claims could not independently verified.The village, located about 15 km northeast of Sanaa in Houthi-controlled territory, suffered extensive damage. Footage aired by Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV showed destroyed homes, thick dust in the air and residents taking shelter in nearby agricultural fields.The footage also showed hospital staff carrying injured children from ambulances. Several children were seen lying on stretchers with bloodied and bandaged bodies as medical staff treated them.Al-Asbahi told Al-Masirah that civilians remained trapped under the rubble. He also alleged that further strikes targeted emergency workers as they tried to rescue survivors.Saturday's airstrikes came a day after an attack on a market in southern Yemen killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials. Both the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed military blamed each other for the attack.The latest violence marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, raising fears that the country could slide back into a prolonged conflict after years of relative calm.The Houthis, who are backed by Iran, control Sanaa and large parts of northern and western Yemen. Their opponents, backed by Saudi Arabia, are based mainly in the south and east.Yemen's war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and forced the internationally recognised government from the capital.Saudi Arabia later led a coalition in support of the government and launched a prolonged air campaign against the rebels, which drew international criticism over civilian casualties.The conflict has killed at least 150,000 people, according to the United Nations. Many more have died from hunger and disease, creating one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.A truce reached in 2022 brought a period of relative calm, but fighting has intensified again since the summer. The Houthis have launched new offensives, saying they were responding to Saudi Arabia's continued blockade of areas under their control.The group has also stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting oil and military infrastructure, as well as shipping in the Red Sea. The Saudi-led coalition, meanwhile, says its airstrikes in Houthi-held areas are aimed at the rebels' military infrastructure.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: First Muslim US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed launches ‘Habibi PAC’ after railing against money in politics
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim US senator-elect, establishes Habibi PAC to combat money in politics and support candidates post-election.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan senator-elect who campaigned on reducing the influence of money in politics, has registered a political action committee days after becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.Named “Habibi PAC”, the committee was registered with the Federal Election Commission on Thursday as a leadership PAC sponsored by El-Sayed, according to Al Jazeera. Such committees allow politicians to raise money independently of their election campaigns and use it to support other candidates, political organisations and activities.The registration comes after El-Sayed used his victory speech to argue that ordinary voters could overcome the influence of wealthy interests. “The many can win,” he said, describing the outcome as a contest between money and the people.The name of the new committee reflects a phrase that became familiar during his campaign. “Habibi”, an Arabic term of affection meaning “my dear” or “my beloved”, was frequently used by El-Sayed while addressing supporters and political opponents.He also directed the expression at Vice President JD Vance during his victory speech in Detroit.“JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you're constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed said.He is not the only newly elected Democrat to establish a leadership PAC after Tuesday's election. Al Jazeera reported that Arizona Congressman-elect Amish Shah registered PACStreet Boy, Iowa Senator-elect Josh Turek launched WheelPAC, and North Carolina Senator-elect Roy Cooper registered One NC PAC.These committees can help lawmakers build political networks by contributing to other candidates and party organisations. They are also used by politicians seeking to develop influence within their parties and strengthen their chances of securing leadership roles or committee chairmanships, according to OpenSecrets, as cited by the news outlet.Leadership PACs distributed $79.3 million to federal candidates during the 2024 election cycle. Republicans received most of the contributions, although a Democratic leadership PAC was the largest individual donor, OpenSecrets data showed.The scale of political spending has also increased during the latest election cycle. OpenSecrets estimated that total expenditure would reach $11.9 billion, compared with $8.9 billion in the 2022 midterms, according to Al Jazeera.Spending by outside groups, largely through super PACs, was projected to reach $3.9 billion, an 85 per cent rise from 2022. Contributions from undisclosed donors, known as dark money, had already crossed $1.47 billion, exceeding the previous record of $1.35 billion set during the 2024 presidential election cycle.El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, defeated Republican Mike Rogers after facing attacks from President Donald Trump, Vance and Senator Ted Cruz. The three called him a “jihadist” and attempted to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood without providing evidence.OpenSecrets also found that conservative groups spent about $360 million more than liberal groups on outside political spending. Democratic candidates, meanwhile, were expected to outspend Republican candidates by around $800 million.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: IAF Gajraj makes world-record landing at 13,629ft in Ladakh
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: An IAF IL-76MD transport aircraft has landed at 13,629 feet in eastern Ladakh, setting a world record for the highest-altitude landing by the
articles.body: SRINAGAR: An IAF IL-76MD transport aircraft has landed at 13,629 feet in eastern Ladakh, setting a world record for the highest-altitude landing by the heavy-lift plane and underscoring India’s growing military airlift capability near the China border.Announcing the achievement Saturday, IAF said the successful landing at Nyoma airbase, barely 25km from the Line of Actual Control, marked “the highest-altitude landing ever achieved by the aircraft anywhere in the world”. Calling it “a remarkable demonstration of the aircraft’s enduring capability, backed by the exceptional skill, precision, and professionalism of its crew”, IAF described the landing as “a milestone that reinforces India’s strategic airlift capability”. At such altitudes, thin air challenges even the most capable aircraft.The Soviet-origin, four-engine Ilyushin aircraft was inducted in 1985 and nicknamed Gajraj. A mainstay of IAF’s transport fleet, it has been used to airlift troops, T-72 tanks, BMP infantry combat vehicles and disaster relief supplies across difficult terrain.Nyoma airbase was earlier an advanced landing ground (ALG) used by tactical transport aircraft and helicopters. The airstrip had remained unused for decades after the 1962 India-China war before IAF reactivated it in Sept 2009. On Sept 18 that year, an AN-32 became the first fixed-wing aircraft to land on its compacted runway.Defence minister Rajnath Singh laid the foundation stone for the airbase in Sept 2023. Completed last year, its upgrade to a fully equipped airbase capable of handling fighter aircraft is expected to strengthen military logistics, improve connectivity to forward areas and speed up the movement of troops and equipment along the China frontier.IAF had earlier reactivated two other airstrips in Ladakh — Daulat Beg Oldi, at 16,614 feet, in May 2008, and Fukche, at 13,000 feet, in Nov 2008.

articles.title: Wangchuk accuses Ladakh admin of witch-hunt & smear campaign
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk Saturday accused the Ladakh administration of “witch-hunting” him for raising his voice for the youth of the
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk Saturday accused the Ladakh administration of “witch-hunting” him for raising his voice for the youth of the country and the well-being of border areas like Ladakh and Arunachal Pradesh.“I am being continuously witch-hunted and defamed and our schools are being harassed in every possible way by the LG administration in Ladakh,” said Wangchuk, who is a member of Leh Apex Body (LAB), a representative body of the people of Ladakh.The Ladakh administration has not responded to the allegations so far.In a message to the President Droupadi Murmu seeking her intervention, Wangchuk alleged, “For the last six years or so, Ladakh has become a police state. We don’t have rights like in the rest of the country, nor democracy.”“Even small comments and likes on social media are a big issue. There are FIRs and even arrests,” he alleged.He said two social media pages, Ladakh Lens 1 and Ladakh Vision 1, surfaced on Oct 14 and that the former allegedly created to defame him through “unfounded allegations” while the latter was aimed at “praising the Lieutenant Governor’s work” in the UT.Wangchuk also alleged that there is “widespread public dissatisfaction with the administration’s policies”.He said the land policy, under which farmers were being stripped of their land and the “industrial and power and tourism policies” favoured corporatisation.He said the govt is promoting liquor bars in every village.He alleged that LG of Ladakh is after institutes like his that have “earned national and international repute”.On Nov 3, authorities directed Himalayan Institute of Alternatives (HIAL), founded by Wangchuk, to refrain from starting classes and other activities at a school within the complex in Leh till a land dispute pending in the high court is decided. A notice pertaining to Desert Flower School was issued to Gitanjali J. Angmo, Wangchuk’s wife who is listed as HIAL’s official founder and CEO. The notice says moves to start classes at the school could “prejudice” proceedings pending in the HC.The school was preparing to begin its new academic session, for which it had sought an NOC that has not been granted so far.According to the govt spokesperson, the notice issued by the Leh tehsildar advises HIAL to maintain “strict status quo” and “not undertake any action whatsoever towards functioning or commencement of activities at the school” until the final HC decision.Ladakh authorities had cancelled HIAL’s land allotment in Aug 2025, following which it moved the HC. In an affidavit last month, the authorities accused HIAL of occupying the land without paying dues.The affidavit also accused Wangchuk of inciting violence in Leh in Sept last year in which four people were killed and scores injured in alleged police firing on protesters demanding statehood and Sixth Schedule status for Ladakh.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Houston mayor says 'elections matter', won't help ICE as Democrats sweep Texas: 'I do this to begin a healing process'
articles.summary: Houston Mayor John Whitmire took a significant step and did not try to distance it from the midterm election result.
articles.body: Houston Mayor John Whitmire took a significant step and did not try to distance it from the midterm election result. He ordered the city's police department to limit cooperation with ICE, saying the move would reduce fear among immigrant communities following the Democrats' victory in Texas elections. "I do this to begin a healing process," he said.Whitmire announced the change on Friday, November 6, days after Democrats secured major victories in the November 3 midterm elections, including Gina Hinojosa's defeat of Republican Governor Greg Abbott and James Talarico defeating Republican Ken Paxton in the US Senate race. The victories ended Republicans' decades-long dominance of statewide offices and changed the political equation for Democratic leaders in the state."I've said many times, elections matter," Whitmire said while announcing the new policy. He said the decision was intended to "reduce fear and anxiety" in Houston, Texas' most populous city.Under the revised policy, Houston police officers conducting routine traffic stops or detaining someone for other reasons will no longer be allowed to notify ICE solely because the individual is subject to a civil immigration warrant. Officers can notify ICE if the person is also arrested and charged with an offence that carries the possibility of jail time."This is the right thing to do at the right time," Whitmire said, adding that he hoped the executive order would become a model for other cities in Texas.Houston Police Chief J Noe Diaz, who joined the mayor at the announcement, said he supported the change and that the department had already begun implementing the new policy.Whitmire said the decision was taken after consultations with Texas' newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller. He said the administration wanted to ensure that immigrants who were working, studying or living with their families did not have to fear routine interactions with local police."We don't want people to worry about their workers, their family members, their students," he said.The mayor also argued that the revised approach was consistent with the stated objective of Texas' Senate Bill 4, which was introduced to prevent so-called sanctuary city policies and target people who commit crimes while in the country illegally.Whitmire, a Democrat who opposed the legislation as a Texas state senator in 2017, had previously backed away from a similar effort to restrict police cooperation with ICE after Abbott threatened to withhold at least $110 million in public safety grants from Houston.The threat came when Houston City Council members sought to introduce a local ordinance giving police officers discretion not to notify ICE when detaining someone subject to a civil immigration warrant. The city eventually withdrew the contentious provision after facing the prospect of losing state funding.However, Whitmire said the political situation had changed following Tuesday's election results. Abbott lost his bid for a fourth term to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is set to become Texas' first Latina governor and the first Democrat to hold the office in more than three decades.The mayor said he was no longer concerned about possible retaliation from the outgoing Republican administration.The policy change comes amid growing tensions over immigration enforcement in Houston, where immigrant-rights groups have accused local police cooperation with ICE of creating fear in immigrant neighbourhoods.Cesar Espinosa, executive director of Houston-based immigrant-rights organisation FIEL, said the previous arrangement had made residents afraid of routine traffic stops and even reporting crimes. He said some residents avoided going to grocery stores because they feared being stopped by police and referred to immigration authorities.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
